title: Pan pipes
summary: Andean pan pipes assembled from published rules, not from a measured instrument: the note set of a zampona (G major), the tube bore scaling of measured panpipes and the lip-jet controls of a skilled player (Fletcher 2005), with each tube's length computed from its note and blown one tube at a time as a stopped pipe filled with exhaled breath. Speaks; not graded on the site. Screened siku recordings now exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches), but the grader has no library for them yet, so the notes are listened to; G4 and B4 were measured against them with the grader's own functions only (see what is missing). No published table of measured siku or zampona tube lengths could be reached, and nothing here claims to match a real instrument.
physics_present: fs-couple flue_loop: a lip jet with the published control ranges (jet speed, lip height and jet length by note) acting on a stopped cylindrical tube
the stopped-pipe resonator: closed at the far end, open at the blown top, with the published bore scaling and the open-end correction
the published stopped-pipe jet offset: the closed end blocks the steady flow so the jet passes outside the lip by half a jet half-width, applied as the labium offset
fractional-delay propagation and gas-derived viscothermal loss along the tube
radiation observed at a physical receiver from the open top

the tubes' gas: exhaled breath (the shared woodwind pack: 27 C, 101325 Pa, saturated, 4.5 percent dry CO2 and 16.5 percent dry O2; Coltman 1966, Nederveen 1969, Fletcher and Rossing 1998), as a played zampona carries it, with the observer and radiation exterior kept as dry air at 20 C. It raises every tube by 10.9 to 11.0 cents (sound speed 345.36 against 343.2 m/s), the level by 0.3 dB, and moves the grader's envelope, harmonic and combined spectral distances to a recording by no more than 0.1 dB; its HNR gap moves by +3.3 dB (G4) and -6.9 dB (B4), but the render has no noise, so its HNR is the solver's numerical floor. The pack is the generic woodwind breath state, the top of its CO2 bracket, not a measurement of a played pan pipe; a played flute measured by Coltman 1968 (about 2.5 percent CO2, 25.8 to 26.5 C) would sit about 5.7 cents higher (unknowns u-bore-gas)
a self-sustained oscillation: each tube settles to a steady tone and re-rendering with another jet seed gives the same pitch and level
physics_missing: a graded comparison: screened siku recordings exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches, 44 valid clips), but the grader's library is built from UIowa-named files and holds none of them, so no pair is graded and the site shows these notes as listening only. Measured directly with the grader's own functions (instrgrade-4, no real-vs-real ruler), G4 against three sikus and B4 against one, the renders sit far from the recordings: spectral centroid 3.0 to 6.8 times too high, upper-harmonic share 10 to 23 dB too high, and an HNR of 65 to 90 dB against the recordings' 9 to 22 dB, because the render has no breath noise. No claim of resemblance is made

measured tube lengths and bores of a real siku or zampona: the lengths are computed from the notes and the bore from a regression on European panpipes. Andean tubes are much less regular, so this is a design from published rules, not a model of an instrument

the even harmonics the published offset should produce: the renders sound odd harmonics only, with a bright, nearly flat run of upper harmonics where a pan pipe has a dominant fundamental. The island's jet is driven hard into saturation by its authored displacement gain and the offset is small beside the swing, so it has no effect; the same limitation as on the flute

pitch: with breath in the tubes the notes land 8.6 to 11.3 cents flat of the tempered design (D3 -9.5, G3 -8.6, D4 -9.1, G4 -10.0, B4 -11.3; dry air gave -19.6 to -22.3). The tube lengths were cut for the speed of sound in dry 20 C air (unknowns u-tube-lengths), and the mouth end correction of the jet and the lip is not the thin-wall value used to cut them. Real sikus are not tuned to equal temperament either: the three G4 recordings measure -12.2, -29.1 and -28.4 cents and the one B4 recording +36.7 cents of the tempered note, so the mean distance of the G4 render from them went from 8.1 (dry) to 13.2 cents (breath) and of the B4 render from 59.0 to 48.0 cents

the jet: the card is an estimate for a lip jet, not a measured jet card, and the jet is short relative to its height, just short of the range where the island's phase correction is exact; the displacement gain is the demonstrator value, the lip aperture width is taken as the tube width, and the jet spreading across the top of the tube is not modelled
the percussive Andean playing style with a turbulent jet; only the normal laminar style is rendered
neighbouring tubes: they are not coupled, nor is the array radiation or the player's lips and face
onset ramp, mouth loss and breath noise: authored, neutral or absent (the bore's gas is the woodwind breath pack, unknowns u-bore-gas)
a radiating outlet at the closed end: the generic input needs one radiating outlet, so a tiny vent of a vanishing fraction of the bore area stands in for it
native verification beyond a single clock and two jet seeds on two notes
